historical_record.description: James A. Martin photographed the property.
The H.S. Crocker Building, an example of the South End's post-earthquake warehouse and industrial reconstruction.

Built at an estimated cost of $80,000 on thick brick footings, replacing a wine warehouse burned in the fire that followed the earthquake. A sawtooth roof of tin and skylights covered the back half; the front windows had tin-covered fire shutters, the chimneys were lined with terra cotta, fireproof vaults for valuables stood in the middle of the building, and sprinklers ran throughout.
Fire damaged the building in 1963 or early 1964; a permit of March 1964 covers cutting out and rebuilding the burnt parts.

Permits through 1964 and early 1965 turned the building from a plain warehouse into a warehouse and Italian salame works: new rooms, a concrete slab poured at the back, a recessed truck dock and a freight elevator.
The second-floor roof was raised to give the Gallo works more clearance, and two openings were cut through the ground floor into 200 Brannan Street next door, one for a conveyor and one for a stair.
San Francisco Heritage's survey called it one of the best brick buildings in the area.
